title: Elements From Odd Places
description: Phosphorus boiled from urine, a quarry that named four elements, and Japan's misplaced element

concepts.title: Cold Fire From Urine
concepts.contentHtml:
One night in 1669, in Hamburg, an alchemist named Hennig Brand was trying to make the philosopher's stone, the fabled substance that would turn base metals into gold. His raw material was urine. By one account he boiled down about 1,200 gallons of it over two weeks into a tar, then heated it with sand and charcoal for hours until a white vapor condensed into waxy drops that glowed in the dark.1

Other accounts give very different amounts. Britannica says he let 50 buckets of urine stand until they putrefied and "bred worms" before boiling them down.2 Years later, when Brand prepared to make phosphorus on a large scale in Hanover, the urine was to come from the local garrison, and reports speak of about 13,000 liters.3 The sources disagree, so the safest figure is simply "a great deal."

The chemistry is sound even though the alchemy was not. Urine carries dissolved phosphates. When the paste is heated strongly, carbon from the charred organic matter pulls the oxygen off the phosphate, and free phosphorus distills away as a vapor. In air the product glows an eerie green and can burst into flame with a garlicky smell, so it was collected under water, where it set solid safely.4

Brand called his find "cold fire" and took it for elemental fire itself; the name phosphorus, Greek for "light bearer," came later. Others profited instead: the merchant Johann Daniel Kraft, the alchemist Johann Kunckel and the philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.5

concepts.title: One Quarry, Four Elements
concepts.contentHtml:
About 20 kilometers northeast of Stockholm, on the island of Resarö, a quarry near the village of Ytterby dug quartz and feldspar for porcelain makers. In 1787 an artillery officer and amateur geologist, Lieutenant Carl Axel Arrhenius, noticed an unusually heavy black rock there. The chemist Johan Gadolin in Turku, Finland, analyzed it and in 1794 reported a new "earth," the old word for a metal oxide, which Anders Ekeberg named yttria. The rock became gadolinite.1

Yttria was not one substance but a crowd. In the early 1840s Carl Gustaf Mosander pulled erbia and terbia out of it, and the two were so alike that chemists later swapped their names.2 In 1878 Jean-Charles de Marignac in Geneva reported two years spent separating a large sample of gadolinite; from the erbium fraction he isolated a new element, ytterbium, which later turned out to hold lutetium as well.3 A sign at the overgrown mine sums it up: yttrium, terbium, erbium and ytterbium were all isolated from its gadolinite and named after Ytterby. Holmium, thulium, gadolinium and tantalum came from its minerals too.4

Why so slow? The rare earths mostly form ions with a +3 charge and are so chemically similar that some textbooks treat them almost as one element. Chemists separated them by fractional crystallization, crystallizing a salt again and again to exploit tiny differences in solubility between neighbors. Many spent whole careers chasing a 99 percent pure sample. The hunt took 160 years, from Arrhenius's rock to 1947, when ion exchange, developed at Oak Ridge and Ames, finally gave a much better way.5

concepts.title: Nipponium: Right Element, Wrong Box
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1904 the Japanese chemist Masataka Ogawa joined William Ramsay's laboratory in London, where Ramsay was combing thorianite, a mineral from Ceylon, for new elements. In December 1905 Ramsay wrote that Ogawa "has discovered a new element, and is engaged in determining its atomic weight, mapping its spectrum, and finding the properties of its salts."1

Ramsay suggested the name nipponium, symbol Np. In 1908 Ogawa announced it, placing it in the empty slot between molybdenum (42) and ruthenium (44), as element 43. Nobody could confirm it. Element 43 was finally made by nuclear reaction in 1937 as technetium, an unstable element. Nipponium was treated as a phantom for nearly 70 years after Ogawa died in 1930, and its symbol went to neptunium.2

The slip was in the arithmetic. Chemists then found an atomic weight from the masses of an element's compounds, which meant assuming their formulas. Ogawa assumed his element formed two bonds, which gave about 100. From 1996 the radiochemist Kenji Yoshihara of Tohoku University, which Ogawa had once led, reread the papers. If the element were rhenium, Ogawa's chloride was really the oxychloride ReOCl4, and his own data then give an atomic weight of 185.2, close to rhenium's 186.2.3

X-ray measurements on his sample, made just before his sudden death, had already pointed the same way but were never published.4 A photographic plate kept by his family shows clear peaks of rhenium, element 75. A 2022 re-examination called the evidence indisputable: Ogawa had rhenium 17 years before a German team reported it in 1925, and simply put it in the wrong box. Some criticisms remain.5

title: Things That Weren't There
description: Polywater, fusion in a jar, and the campaign to ban dihydrogen monoxide

concepts.title: Polywater: The Water That Wasn't
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1962 Nikolai Fedyakin, working in the Soviet city of Kostroma, was studying pure liquids in glass capillaries about 0.003 mm wide. Over a month, a short column of a second liquid appeared at the top of some tubes, and it was denser than the water below. Boris Deryagin's laboratory in Moscow took up the work, and its "modified water" froze at about -30 °C, boiled at 250 °C and was 15 times more viscous than the ordinary kind.1

The West noticed late, then went wild. In 1969 a team from the National Bureau of Standards and the University of Maryland reported spectra suggesting the stuff was a polymer of water molecules, and the name polywater stuck, even though the samples were microscopic.2 The world's whole supply would barely have filled a thimble, yet a physicist at Wilkes College warned that once let loose, it might feed on natural water and turn Earth into a "reasonable facsimile of Venus."3

The answer lay in the glass and on the skin. In 1970 the Bell Labs chemist Denis Rousseau played a hard game of handball, wrung out his sweaty T-shirt, evaporated the sweat to a gummy residue and found that its infrared spectrum looked like polywater's. Tests on Deryagin's own samples had found organic contaminants such as lipids, and porous glass can soak up the faint haze of salts that every person gives off.4 In a tube that thin, a trace of dirt is a big share of the sample. In 1973 Deryagin agreed that the odd properties came from impurities: even the cleanest samples held silicon or other contaminants.5 Polywater was water carrying dissolved glass and grime.

concepts.title: Fusion in a Jar
concepts.contentHtml:
On March 23, 1989, the University of Utah presented work that its president, Chase Peterson, ranked "right up there with fire, the cultivation of plants, and with electricity." Two chemists, Stanley Pons and Martin Fleischmann, said that by running a current through heavy water, rich in the hydrogen isotope deuterium, they had fused nuclei at room temperature and released heat. Physicists balked: nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, which is why fusion normally needs the extreme temperatures and pressures inside the Sun or an H-bomb. At a physics meeting on May 1, Steven Koonin of Caltech said: "We're suffering from the incompetence and, perhaps, delusion of Professors Pons and Fleischmann."1

Labs everywhere tried palladium electrodes in heavy water, and most found neither excess heat nor fusion products. The missing products were the giveaway: deuterium fusion throws out neutrons and tritium, by far its most sensitive signatures, and even labs that reported heat found nowhere near enough of them. The heat itself was shaky: in closed cells, where all the gas made by electrolysis was recombined, most experimenters saw no excess heat at all. In November 1989 a Department of Energy panel judged the evidence for a new nuclear process "not persuasive."2

The idea never quite died; its remaining researchers now speak of low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR). Google funded a fresh, careful search from 2015,3 and in 2019 the teams reported that their efforts had yet to yield any evidence of cold fusion, though they learned new things about metals packed with hydrogen.4 In 2022 the US Department of Energy offered up to $10 million to settle whether LENR could ever become a carbon-free energy source.5

concepts.title: The Deadly Chemical Called Water
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1997 Nathan Zohner, a 14-year-old at Eagle Rock Junior High School in Idaho Falls, handed 50 ninth-graders a warning about dihydrogen monoxide. It is colorless, odorless and tasteless, it said, and kills uncounted thousands of people every year, mostly by accidental inhalation. Its solid form causes severe tissue damage, and it has been found in tumors of terminal cancer patients. Forty-three students voted to ban it, six were undecided, and only one recognized it as plain water. His project, "How Gullible Are We?", won first prize at the Greater Idaho Falls Science Fair.1

Every line was true. The name literally means "two hydrogen, one oxygen": it is H2O. Nor was the joke new; a Michigan newspaper, the Durand Express, reportedly ran a DHMO scare as an April Fool's prank in 1983.2 Accidental inhalation is drowning, the damage from the solid form is frostbite, and every tumor contains water. The trick is selection: list only the harms, use an unfamiliar name and leave out the dose.

It works on adults too. In 2004 the city of Aliso Viejo, California, was set to ban polystyrene cups after a city paralegal concluded that this chemical, used in making them, could "threaten human safety and health."3 In 2007 the New Zealand MP Jacqui Dean signed a letter asking whether the government's drug experts had a view on banning the "drug."4 The fear behind the joke is real. In a survey of 5,631 people in eight European countries, almost a third said they were afraid of chemicals, and almost 40% said they would like to live in a world where chemical substances do not exist.5 Water itself is a chemical.

title: Brilliant and Deadly
description: Midgley's leaded gas and CFCs, the Radium Girls' glowing paint, and mercury-poisoned hatters

concepts.title: Thomas Midgley: Leaded Gas, Then CFCs
concepts.contentHtml:
By late October 1924, the men making a new gasoline additive at Standard Oil's Bayway refinery in New Jersey were being poisoned by it. Five died and 35 were hospitalized, many of them driven insane by lead. The additive's inventor, General Motors researcher Thomas Midgley Jr., had already lost the whole of February 1923 to illness from its fumes.1 On October 30 he faced reporters in New York and poured the liquid, tetraethyl lead, over his hands to show it was safe.2

The chemistry did what it promised. A small dose of the lead compound stopped engine knock, fuel exploding too early in the cylinder, so engines could run harder. GM next asked Midgley for a refrigerant that would neither poison nor burn. Within three days he had a chlorofluorocarbon, or CFC, later sold as Freon.

Both worked too well. CFCs were so unreactive that nothing in the lower air broke them down, so they drifted up to the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light tore off their chlorine atoms, which destroy ozone. One chemical engineer calls Midgley "the king of unintended consequences."3 Lead, meanwhile, came out of exhaust pipes and settled into air, soil and children. A 2022 study estimated that childhood exposure to leaded gas cost more than 170 million Americans a collective 824 million IQ points; US cars burned it until 1996.4 Midgley never learned what his inventions had done. Polio took the use of his legs, and at 55 he was strangled by the ropes of a pulley system he had built to lift himself out of bed.5

concepts.title: The Radium Girls: Paint That Settled in Bone
concepts.contentHtml:
From 1917 a factory in Orange, New Jersey, painted watch dials with Undark, a paint that glowed in the dark because it mixed a trace of radium with zinc sulfide: radiation from the radium made the crystals shine. The painters were mostly young women. To keep a fine point on their brushes they used a trick called lip pointing, shaping the tip between their lips, which meant swallowing a little radium with every dial.1

They were assured the radium would simply pass through them. It did not. Chemically, radium behaves enough like calcium that the body builds it into bone, where it goes on irradiating the living tissue around it. The first signs were in the mouth: rotting teeth, persistent pain and jawbones that were dying.2

In June 1928 five former painters, including Grace Fryer, settled their suit against the United States Radium Corporation for $10,000 each, a $600 yearly annuity and their medical costs. The company never admitted liability.3 Their suffering also set the first safety limit. A 1941 federal handbook fixed the most radium a worker's body should carry at 0.1 microgram, a level its authors chose because they would be comfortable if their own wives and daughters were the subjects.4 When the Manhattan Project began handling new radioactive elements that turned out to behave in the body much like radium, one of its leading scientists, Glenn Seaborg, remembered the dial painters and insisted on research and strict safety rules.5

concepts.title: Mad Hatters: Real Poison, Doubtful Hatter
concepts.contentHtml:
Felt hats began with a bath of poison. In carroting, rabbit or beaver fur was washed in an orange solution of mercury nitrate, which loosened the fur from the pelt and made it shrink and mat together into felt. In the hat factories of Danbury, Connecticut, workers also breathed the mercury as vapor and dust.1

Mercury vapor passes from the lungs into the blood and on to the brain. Long exposure brings a classic triad: tremor, inflamed gums and erethism, a change of personality marked by excessive shyness, irritability and outbursts of temper.2 The toll was heavy. A 1922 study by Alice Hamilton found that of 100 union hatters examined in Danbury, 43 had mercury poisoning.3

Medicine did not end it. Mercury left American hat making only in 1941, when the metal was needed for detonators in the Second World War, and a 1989 study of New Jersey's hatters argues that the idea of "mad" hatters came more from popular perception than from medical knowledge.4 As for Lewis Carroll's Hatter in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865), the diagnosis is doubtful. The phrase "mad as a hatter" was in print by 1837, and Carroll's character may have been a caricature of Theophilus Carter, an eccentric furniture dealer who was not a hat maker and never worked with mercury.5 The poisoning was real; the Hatter's madness is probably just Carroll's comedy.

title: Happy Accidents
description: Saccharin on a dinner roll, Teflon in a cylinder that gave no gas, and thioacetone's stench

concepts.title: Saccharin: Sweetness on a Dinner Roll
concepts.contentHtml:
As the story is told, one evening in June, after a day in the laboratory, the chemist Constantin Fahlberg sat down to dinner, picked up a roll and found its crust remarkably sweet. He had spilled an experimental compound on his hands. He ran back to the lab and tasted everything on his workbench, vials and dishes included, until he found the source: an overboiled beaker in which a reaction had produced the compound now called saccharin.1 The lab belonged to Ira Remsen at Johns Hopkins University, and the year was 1878.2

The two men were co-discoverers and published the find together in 1879. Then, in 1884, without telling Remsen, Fahlberg patented a cheaper way to make it, and in 1886 he filed more patents claiming to be the sole discoverer of "Fahlberg's saccharin." Remsen, who wanted recognition rather than money, protested to the chemistry community.3

Because the body barely breaks it down, saccharin gives sweetness without calories. Its next fight was over safety. In the 1970s rats fed large doses developed bladder tumors, and a US ban loomed. In 1977 Congress instead passed the Saccharin Study and Labeling Act, which put a warning label on every saccharin product and blocked a ban for two years.4 Later research showed that the way saccharin causes cancer in rats does not apply in humans, and in 2000 it was removed from the US government's list of substances reasonably anticipated to cause cancer.5

concepts.title: Teflon: The Gas That Never Came Out
concepts.contentHtml:
Roy Plunkett's first job at DuPont was to make new versions of the refrigerant Freon, Midgley's CFC. On April 6, 1938, he and his technician Jack Rebok opened a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene gas that they had filled themselves, and nothing came out. Yet the cylinder was too heavy to be empty. Risking an explosion, they cut it open and found that the gas had turned into a white powder.

Plunkett set his planned work aside to test it. It was more slippery than graphite, almost no chemical touched it, and it melted only when very hot. The small gas molecules had linked into long chains, a polymer called polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), whose carbon backbone is wrapped in a sheath of fluorine atoms. By 1941 it had a trade name, Teflon, and Plunkett had been moved on to supervise DuPont's tetraethyl lead production.1 By the thinking of the day, the powder should not have formed: chemists had decided that this gas could not polymerize.2

PTFE was so expensive that it seemed it would never find a market, until the Manhattan Project needed materials that could resist the corrosive fluorine compounds of its uranium enrichment plant.3 Its slipperiness comes from that fluorine sheath. The carbon-fluorine bond is among the strongest single bonds in chemistry, so the surface does not react.4 Fluorine also holds its electrons so tightly that other molecules feel almost no pull toward it, leaving egg and grease nothing to grip. There is a catch: that durability means PTFE lasts for ages, and chemicals once used to make it, such as PFOA, have polluted the environment.5

concepts.title: Thioacetone: A Smell Measured in Quarter-Miles
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1889, chemists in the German university town of Freiburg tried to make a small sulfur compound, thioacetone. A later English account of their report says the work released "an offensive smell which spread rapidly over a great area of the town causing fainting, vomiting and a panic evacuation." An 1890 report from a soap works in Leeds called the odor "fearful."1 The story reaches us through retellings, so the scale of the panic is hard to check.

In the 1960s chemists at Esso's research station in Abingdon, England, studied the compound as a route to new polymers and met the smell for themselves. A stopper popped out of a bottle of residues for a moment, and colleagues in a building 200 yards away complained of nausea. Two chemists who had handled only minute amounts had a waitress spray deodorant around them in a restaurant.2 In a test, observers were posted at distances of up to a quarter of a mile while a single drop sat in a fume cupboard. Downwind, they smelled it within seconds.3

Thioacetone is acetone with its oxygen swapped for sulfur. A carbon-sulfur double bond is weak, so the free molecule rarely survives: it locks up with two others into a ring-shaped trimer, and nobody is sure whether the stench comes from thioacetone itself or a close relative.4 Our noses are tuned to sulfur. People can smell the thiol added to natural gas at 0.3 parts per billion, probably because such compounds come from rotting food. Thiols are also called mercaptans, from the Latin for "capturing mercury," the metal from the hatters' story.5
